Simulacra is a visual novel with some minor horror elements told through a phone.

The basic story is woman goes missing and you end up with her phone. You go through it opening apps, texts, emails, etc, attempting to track her down.

The gameplay is divided into 2 main sections. The first is texting back and forth with people in her text/dating apps. The 2nd section is puzzle based where you need to find/figure out some piece of information to proceed. The game gives you little hints in what you should currently be looking for.

On the plus side: There's some branching paths in response choices that can lead to amusing things happening with various characters. It has multiple endings. Puzzles are actually fairly decent. There're some easter eggs/other things you can mess around with and be amused by.

Looking at the downsides of this: Once you have the whole picture of what's going on, the plot and parts of the story don't make much sense in how they would've play out. The characters aren't that good and one of them is written to be unlikable. Occasionally you'll get video messages and the acting certainly isn't good. Occasional misspellings or responses that don't make much sense. The horror element is more of a background thing, so don't expect it to stand out and be prevalent throughout.

Overall, it's a decent visual novel with some options to fool around with. It's not exceptional in any way, but it's different than standard VRs and has some actual gameplay elements to it, which is nice.

It has its moments. You're interacting with a girl's phone to try and find out what's happened to her. A fun idea for a mystery game, I thought.  At first the game seems to invite you to try to play ethically, meaning, don't lie to any of her contacts. I tried that but then discovered I was failing certain objectives. You're supposed to lie to achieve the intended good outcomes of the game. But before I understood that, when I was trying to play being as honest as possible, I felt like I was being forced to make certain unethical choices. Since I felt like I was being railroaded, I just started doing ridiculous stuff, which led to the game's bad ending. So, on the plus side, my choices really did have consequences. But the problem is the developers' intentions were unclear. I wish I'd known at the beginning of the game what I now understand to be failure and success according to the game's system. I would have enjoyed it a lot more.

The game has a horror element, which is mainly just cheap jump scares. I wouldn't mind them so much if they hadn't mixed the audio so that the jump scare moments are twice as loud as the rest of the game. It's not scary; it's just annoying. I kept having to adjust the volume up and down to avoid the speakers blasting. They ask you to wear headphones because they want the sound to blast in your ears, I guess. There were a few times when the horror was genuinely earned as a result of caring for the characters and a growing understanding of what was at stake, helped along by a few subtle effects. Those were good times...

There's some fun commentary on the inevitable erasure of life as we know it through globalized tech, transhumanism, and 4IR. The fake cyber attack and the resulting driver's license for the internet is the next step, folks! ( ๑ ᴖ ᴈ ᴖ)★

I don't know what qualities I should look for when reviewing horror games, but as someone who has been keen on horror games since childhood, I really enjoyed the game.
Jump-scares are unexpected and frightening, but it was the distorted faces and voices in the glitched videos that really struck me as "scary."

As for the points I don't like:
•Acting sucks. There were scenes that I cringed a lot while watching. Even the text messages are cringe... Like, there are literally missing people out there, and yet everyone uses weird emojis in every damn message.
•As someone who loves choice-based games, only a few of your choices affect the ending, and the game has only 4 different endings (which is way less than I expected.)
•I don't want to spoil the endings, but I must say, I didn't like any of them.
•The phone interface is not good. Its functionality is pretty limited. Chatting is slow, you can't switch between tabs; you can't use the tab button on the keyboard to switch between text boxes, and you can't start videos from a certain timestamp.

Other than these, it's definitely a fun and spooky experience. The price is totally acceptable for 5 hours (and multiple playthroughs with a new game+ / fast chatting mode), so I recommend it.

The setting is a good idea. They are achieving a good ambiance with background noises that are really well mixed.
This is the only positive point in my experience.

The actual gameplay is very linear and highly undynamic. The investigation part of the game feels more like a checklist then actually trying to understand the persons involved. Why is that? The characters are all very plain and are represented in bad writing. They feel stereotypical to a point were I was only annoyed by their presence and had to figure out how to deal with their stupidity. Their language felt really unnatural and to top it off some video clips and voice calls to top it all off.
There were some interesting ideas, but in general the game feels rushed in really unpolished.
The options of dialogue were pretty straight forward, but as I already said it there are little subbranches to discover. The decision you make are making minor differences in the end scene. The achievements are less of a challenge, more a lure into replaying a game that has little to no replay value.

To finalize. Yes I agree that the concept is nice, but this game clearly lacks quality. Instead of trying to polish the game, they just move on the next. So Simulacra is left in a very bare bones state in the end.

Simulacra is a "found phone" psychological mystery / horror game where your curiosity has gotten you involved with a mystery... You found this phone on your doorstep. You initially have no idea what to enter, then the phone glitched and revealed its passcode. You find chat logs, call logs, and the owner was Anna. There was a corrupted video where a terrified Anna screamed that don't come after her... Then the message was cut off. 

As you scan the phone's various steps for clues, and maybe even engage in some social engineering with Anna's friends, including (ex-?) boyfriend Greg, bestie Ashley, and dating app date Taylor, you need to reconstruct Anna's life before she went missing, to have a chance at finding out what happened to her...  

The videos are very high quality, but the simulated phone calls don't sound nearly as good. 

The special effects where the phone glitched got the definitely horror feel to it. Same with the time-warp feel when the phone really glitches out. 

The puzzles such as the sentence scramble and photo scramble doesn't quite fit into the gameplay though.  The "sentence scramble" feels a bit of "make work". Same with the photo scramble. 

There seems to be a lot of alternative paths one can take, so there would be a lot of additional achievements should you want a replay or two. 

All puzzles have clues accessible within the phone itself, though some may be more obscure than others. Part of the fun is to figure out the rest. And there are a lot of red herrings. 

All in all, interesting mechanic for a puzzle game and gradual revelation, if you dig this sort of game.

Simulacra is a found phone simulator. Apparently that's a genre now. 

On a phone, the premise of Simulacra is something special: What if your phone turned into someone else's phone, and you could hack into it to snoop out all the little things about our life that we entrust to our phones these days. And because said phone gives you complete access to the online persona of the owner of that phone, you also get to moonlight as an online predator. 

It still works well enough on the PC, although the immersion is somewhat diminished. 

But hey, it's OK, because Anna, the owner of the phone, is in trouble and you are the only one with access to enough information to maybe help her. And also…  this is just a game. 

If I sound like I'm down on the game for the icky things it expects you to do, I'm actually not. The game never shies away from pointing out how questionable the means you employ are, and if you want it, you can go about things in the most ethical way possible. You won't get the best ending, though. 

The actual means by which the game let's you morally compromise yourself are quite simple. Some light social hacking, catfishing, actual hacking, two simple mini-games. The rest of the time you read dialogue or watch a few videos with above average novice actors, and thus follow along a nifty little horror story whose ending felt very rushed but still packed quite a punch. 

The game is a bit railroady, though. The main thing you do is converse with Anna's contacts via multiple choice chat, and oftentimes the few options you have are very obviously pushing the story in the direction it wants to go. Thanks to the brevity of the game, this never gets too grating, though. 

The main freight of meaning and engagement this game transported for me was the fun and glee you can actually get out of pretending to be a terrible person with access to someone else's phone, and thinking about what that actually means for the hellscape we are all constructing for ourselves. There is no way around it: If you have no moral compass, being a troll is a very good time. Good thing then that in Simulacra, the moral justification comes with the box. 

TLDR: Interesting little title whose premise and insinuations become more horrifying the longer you think about it. Bit on the short side, but well worth experiencing.

In the Simulacra games, you’re put into the role of a person who gets in possession of a mobile phone, and you have to solve puzzles in order to figure out what happened to its original owner. I’m lumping these two games together because even though their narratives aren’t connected to any great degree, the overall concept and gameplay is identical for both games.

In general, the Simulacra games remind me a lot of how the Orwell games work, in the sense that much of what you do is rifle through personal data. What’s different is that in these games you’re an active participant and not just an observer, so you get to talk to various characters directly, instead of just listening into their conversations.

Now just finding a phone and looking through its contents isn’t that interesting, most people in general aren’t interesting. But both games start with video messages from the original owners that indicate that something sinister is going on, and that’s where the FMV sequences come into play. 

For what it’s worth, these sequences aren’t played out of some misguided, ironic attempt at nostalgia like many other FMV games. It’s more just a representation of how we use our phones in real life. Video isn’t just a gimmick here, it’s part of what the games need to have in order to tell their stories.

Unfortunately, the acting during these FMV sequences isn’t that great. The first game does come off a bit better because it’s mostly centered around online dating, so there are only a few videos or instances of video calls that happen, but the second game targets influencer culture, where video plays a much bigger role. And there are also video sequences that happen outside of the context of the phone, because this is a sequel and I guess that’s a way of telling your customers that it’s worth buying another one because it has more stuff than the previous one. As a result, the unconvincing acting takes up much more runtime.

And I do have to say that the second game really hams it up a notch. It’s difficult to tell if the acting quality is intentional, since the second game is a rather scathing takedown of influencer culture, it could also be a jab at the terrible acting influencers employ during their fake drama.

The writing is pretty decent for the most part. I mean, these are cheesy horror games mostly about millennials, so you’re not really expecting F. Scott Fitzgerald quality stuff here, but it still manages to convey a sense of personality, even to some of the characters whose voices you never get to hear. Though I have to say that the second game has this weird idea of making every single character you have to investigate a complete as[i][/i]shole. I guess this comes with the territory for professional influencers. But if you, like me, watch cheesy 80’s slasher movies in order to see smug teenagers die in creative ways without having to empathize with them, it’s weird for the game to then turn around and give you a bad ending for wanting to punish these self-centered jerks. To get the good ending and also not miss out on a bunch of actual puzzles and therefore content, you have to stroke their egos quite a bit and metaphorically appeal to the power of friendship to solve the mystery.

Overall I like the gameplay of the second game more, because it offers a broader set of mechanics, but I liked the more nuanced characters in the first game better because not everyone there is just a despicable manipulative as[i][/i]shole. But in general, they’re nice time killers and they’re fully intended to be played through multiple times to get to see everything. And the nice thing is that the developers even implemented a fast-forward feature for repeat playthroughs so you can get through the text conversations faster, which was much appreciated. So yeah, if you want a modern example of how an FMV game can work and you can stomach some stilted acting and don’t mind the presence of generally dislikable characters, I’d recommend these games, they’re a fun little distraction.
